doc.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

title: Cannonball Adderley live tape and what he was like
summary: Monk Rowe plays Cannonball's Stars Fell on Alabama from a club tape. Dorn praises Cannonball as a musician and a smart man, and defends his commercial work.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: I don’t know if this will be a surprise. I don’t think so.
At least I hope I’ll know what it is. I guessed one of them, right?
[audio interlude]
It’s one of my favorite records I’ve ever made. See this is what happens in a club.
Check this out.

Johnny Hodges where are you? Well you know that’s Cannon — “Stars Fell on Alabama” and he had done that on the Riverside, you know the studio version, but I had heard him do that in a club and when I got these tapes from Allen Grant I listened and I said, oh man, Cannon playing “Stars Fell on Alabama.” You hear what he plays? That’s why them called him the new Bird for that first year. I heard some Bird the other day you’ve never heard. It’s spectacular. A guy’s apartment in 1950.
Wow.

He takes a solo on “Fine and Dandy,” in a jam session in a guy’s apartment, there is Bird that is equal to that, there is no better Bird. So now I’m going to try and find a place for that. A cat brought it by like a week or two ago. But Cannon man—
Yeah. What was he like?

He was absolutely brilliant. He was a spectacular musician. Real hall of famer, right up there with the best of whoever did it. But he was smart and he was glib and he was learned and he was school-smart and street-smart. I learned a lot from him. A lot from him. A lot of guys resented his commercial success. They said he was a cop out or stuff like that. Let me tell you something. From the beginning when he and Nat first went out, you know with —
Their own quintet?

Their own quintet, that Jazz Workshop with “This Here,” the Bobby Timmon song and San Francisco. Through the end of the second quartet, or the second sextet, when he had — what is it, that sextet he had with Yusef — did you ever hear that group?
Oh yeah.
You saw them?
Oh I didn’t see them, no.

Wow. The group with Charles Lloyd was good. But the one with Yusef, other than the Miles sextet with Cannon and Trane, that’s my favorite sextet of all time. Nat, Cannon, Yusef, Zawinul, Sam Jones and Louis Hayes. They could play anything.
Isn’t that the group that did the recording of “Gemini” with that marvelous thing in the middle of it that knocks people out.
Oh man. Cannon — first of all Cannon knew how to work an audience. He was brilliant. He was brilliant. He could do anything. And like boy and boy was he smart. He was a good guy too.
Yeah, and what a tone.

Because he was so successful, guys put him down. And he did commercial stuff. You listen to “Nippon Soul,” “Brother John,” stuff like that — you want to hear what Cannon could do? And he wasn’t in Miles’ sextet by mistake. Miles, Trane and Cannon. That’s a front line, isn’t it?
I guess so. We won’t see that again.
No we won’t. Ever.
